text: The Padma Bhushan (IAST: Padma Bhūṣaṇa, lit. 'Lotus Decoration') is the third-highest civilian award in the Republic of India, coming after the Bharat Ratna and the Padma Vibhushan and before the Padma Shri. Instituted on 2 January 1954, it is awarded for "distinguished service of a high order...without distinction of race, occupation, position or sex," including service in any field such as that rendered by government servants, with exceptions for those working in public sector undertakings, except doctors and scientists. As of 2025, the award has been conferred upon 1341 individuals, including 38 posthumous and 101 non-citizen recipients. The recommendations for the award are submitted annually between 1 May and 15 September by state and union territory governments, Ministries of the Government of India, Bharat Ratna and Padma Vibhushan awardees, Institutes of Excellence, Ministers, Chief Ministers, Governors, Members of Parliament, and private individuals. These recommendations are processed by the Padma Awards Committee, convened annually by the Prime Minister of India, which then submits its findings to the Prime Minister and the President of India for approval. Recipients are announced on 26 January, the Republic Day of India, and their names are registered in The Gazette of India, a weekly publication by the Department of Publication, Ministry of Urban Development, which is required for the conferral to be considered official. Recipients whose awards are revoked or restored—both actions requiring presidential authority—must surrender their medals when their names are struck from the register. Initially, the award was not given posthumously, but this was changed in the January 1955 statute; D. C. Kizhakemuri became the first posthumous recipient in 1999. The original design featured a silver circle 1+3⁄8 inches (35 mm) in diameter with a lotus flower embossed on the obverse and "Padma Bhushan" in Devanagari script above it, a floral wreath on the lower edge, and the State Emblem of India on the reverse with "Desh Seva" in Devanagari script on the lower edge, suspended by a pink ribbon 1+1⁄4 inches (32 mm) wide with two white vertical lines. In 1955, the design was modified to a bronze-toned medallion 1+3⁄4 inches (44 mm) in diameter and 1⁄8 inch (3.2 mm) thick, with a central raised circular space and a lotus flower, "Padma" above and "Bhushan" below, and the State Emblem on the reverse with "Satyameva Jayate" in Devanagari script. The rim and all embossing are in standard gold with "Padma Bhushan" in gold gilt, and the ribbon has a broad white stripe in the middle. The award ranks fifth in the order of precedence for wearing medals and decorations and is produced at the Alipore Mint, Kolkata, alongside other civilian and military awards. The Padma Bhushan, along with other personal civil honours, was briefly suspended twice: from July 1977 to January 1980 and from August 1992 to December 1995. The first suspension occurred when Morarji Desai became Prime Minister, criticized as "worthless and politicized," and was rescinded on 25 January 1980 after Indira Gandhi took office. The second suspension followed two Public-Interest Litigations in 1992—one in the Kerala High Court by Balaji Raghavan and another in the Madhya Pradesh High Court (Indore Bench) by Satya Pal Anand—questioning the awards as "titles" under Article 18 of the Constitution. On 25 August 1992, the Madhya Pradesh High Court issued a temporary suspension. A Special Division Bench of the Supreme Court, comprising A. M. Ahmadi C. J., Kuldip Singh, B. P. Jeevan Reddy, N. P. Singh, and S. Saghir Ahmad, restored the awards on 15 December 1995, ruling that the Bharat Ratna and Padma awards are not titles under Article 18. Several recipients have refused or returned the award: Sisir Bhaduri (1959) refused, stating that state awards create a sycophantic environment and do not reflect the government's seriousness about theatre; Vilayat Khan declined in 1968, citing incompetent selection committees, having previously refused the Padma Shri in 1964 and the Padma Vibhushan in 2000; Nikhil Chakravarty rejected it in 1990, saying journalists should not be identified with the establishment; Romila Thapar declined twice—first in 1992 and again in 2005—stating she would accept awards only from academic institutions or those linked to her professional work, and sent a clarification letter to President A. P. J. Abdul Kalam explaining her prior refusal; K. Subrahmanyam refused his 1999 award, arguing bureaucrats and journalists should not accept government awards due to potential favouritism; Dattopant Thengadi (RSS volunteer) rejected the 2003 award until K. B. Hedgewar and M. S. Golwalkar were offered the Bharat Ratna; S. R. Sankaran turned down the 2005 award without explanation; S. Janaki refused in 2013, stating the award came late in her five-and-a-half-decade career and requesting more recognition for southern artists; family members of J. S. Verma, the 27th Chief Justice of India, refused the posthumous award, saying Verma would not have accepted it as he never sought acclaim; K. Shivaram Karanth returned his 1968 award in protest against the 1975 Emergency; Khushwant Singh returned his 1974 award in 1984 in protest against Operation Blue Star, later receiving the Padma Vibhushan in 2007; Pushpa Mittra Bhargava returned his 1986 award in 2015 in protest against the Dadri mob lynching and due to concerns about the socio-political climate. In 2010, Indian-American businessman Sant Singh Chatwal was awarded the Padma Bhushan in the field of Public Affairs, which sparked controversy due to his guilty plea for violating the Federal Election Campaign Act and witness tampering in the 2008 U.S. presidential election, and allegations of lobbying for the award through contacts in the Prime Minister's Office and U.S. Congress. The government clarified that Chatwal is a "tireless advocate" of India's interests abroad and stated that a due diligence process was conducted, with three of five CBI-registered cases against him closed by the CBI and two others resulting in his discharge by courts, with no adverse records found. Media reports indicate several cases filed after April 2009, including three with Kerala Police and four in Delhi and Kerala High Courts, and Chatwal received a summons in January 2010; however, Union Home Secretary Gopal Krishna Pillai stated no probe had been ordered or report sought. In 2008, Chatwal was considered for the Padma Shri but the Indian Embassy in Washington, D.C. declined to nominate him, citing controversy over his financial dealings and that his contributions were less significant than others, and that the award would demoralize those who had done more and create the impression that lack of transparency disqualifies individuals from honours. In 2022, former West Bengal Chief Minister Buddhadeb Bhattacharya refused his award on the eve of the 73rd Republic Day, reportedly not being intimated about his nomination and publicly stating that if he had been awarded, he would refuse it; his name appeared on the official list, and he has since refused the award.
